#### State as a fold — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** What "state" actually is, and why persisting it is an optimisation — as one `buildFrom` function called two ways.

`entryOf(e)` is the unit: a **(key, window)** pair. 9 events produce 7 of them, so the state this whole chapter is about is 7 numbers.

Step 2 is the point: `full.readCount` = 9 and `resume.readCount` = 4, and both hold the same 7 entries. Step 4 is the cost — `collectableAt("a@480")` returns NONE, so one entry is never freed, and persistence makes that leak survive restarts.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-why-memory/ch07-why-memory.svg" alt="State as a fold — stack and heap at every step, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — state is one number per (key, window) pair</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-why-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: state is one number per (key, window) pair" width="980">

`id` is `"a@480"` — a key and a window start, nothing else. 9 events produce 7 such ids, so "state" is 7 numbers. Everything in this chapter exists to carry those 7 numbers across a restart.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — resuming from a checkpoint reads fewer events, same result</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-why-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: resuming from a checkpoint reads fewer events, same result" width="980">

`full.readCount` is 9 and `resume.readCount` is 4 — and both States hold the same 7 entries. Persistence changed the cost and not the answer, which is why it is an optimisation rather than a correctness mechanism.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — the fold runs one way: the entries do not name their events</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-why-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: the fold runs one way: the entries do not name their events" width="980">

Entry `a@0` holds 8, built from 2 events. Nothing in `st.entries` records which events — so stream → state is a function and state → stream is not. That asymmetry is why losing state is survivable and losing the stream is not.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and 1 entry is never collectable at all</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-why-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and 1 entry is never collectable at all" width="980">

`collectableAt("a@480")` returns NONE — the loop runs out without any watermark reaching 600. Its 8 stays allocated for the life of the job. Before persistence a restart cleared such an entry by accident; a durable store checkpoints it and restores it faithfully, forever.

</details>
